example.problem: Initially A=10 and B=5. The log is: T1 start, T1 writes A from 10 to 20, T2 start, T2 writes B from 5 to 7, T1 commit. The system then crashes. What are A and B after recovery?
steps: T1 has a commit record, so it is a winner and its write is redone: A becomes 20.
T2 has no commit record, so it is a loser and its write is undone: B returns to its old value, 5.
The database now shows only the effect of the committed transaction.
example.result: A = 20 and B = 5.

misconceptions: Not every logged transaction is redone: only those with a commit record. A transaction that started and wrote but did not commit is undone.
Recovery is idempotent: redo and undo can be repeated, so after a crash during recovery the same redo and undo lists are used again and the database stays consistent.

recall.q: What does write-ahead logging require?
recall.a: The log record for an update must reach stable storage before the updated data page does.

recall.q: Which transactions are redone after a crash?
recall.a: Those with a commit record in the log, after the last checkpoint.

recall.q: Which value is used to undo a write?
recall.a: The old value (before-image) stored in the update record.

practice.stem: Initially A=100, B=200, C=300. The log is: T1 start; T1 A 100 to 150; T2 start; T2 B 200 to 260; checkpoint {T1,T2}; T1 commit; T3 start; T3 C 300 to 310; T2 A 150 to 170; T2 commit. The system crashes here. After recovery, what is A + B + C?
practice.explanation: T1 and T2 have commit records, so their writes are redone, giving A=170 (T2's later write) and B=260. T3 has none, so its write to C is undone and C=300. The sum is 170 + 260 + 300 = 730. Answering 740 is tempting if you keep T3's write to C as if it were durable.

lesson.summary: Redo transactions with a commit record, undo those without, and begin at the last checkpoint. Old values restore losers and new values rebuild winners.

formulas.name: Number of schedules (interleavings)
where: number of operations of transaction T_i
formulas.note: Concurrent (non-serial) schedules are N − k!. Two transactions of 3 operations each give 20 − 2 = 18.

formulas.name: When two operations conflict
formulas.tex: p \text{ conflicts with } q \iff T(p) \ne T(q) \,\land\, \mathrm{item}(p) = \mathrm{item}(q) \,\land\, (p = w \lor q = w)
formulas.text: p conflicts with q ⟺ different transactions ∧ same item ∧ at least one is a write

formulas.name: Conflict-serializability test
formulas.tex: S \text{ is conflict serializable} \iff G(S) \text{ is acyclic}
formulas.text: S is conflict serializable ⟺ precedence graph G(S) is acyclic
where: precedence graph: edge Ti → Tj when an op of Ti conflicts with a later op of Tj
formulas.note: Equivalent serial schedules are exactly the topological orders of G(S).

formulas.name: Recoverability hierarchy
formulas.note: Independent of serializability: a serial schedule is strict, but a conflict-serializable schedule need not even be recoverable.

formulas.name: Serializability hierarchy
formulas.note: The gap between conflict and view serializability consists of schedules with blind writes.

formulas.name: Timestamp ordering: read rule
formulas.tex: r_T(X) \text{ rolls back } T \iff TS(T) < W\text{-}TS(X); \text{ else } R\text{-}TS(X) \leftarrow \max(R\text{-}TS(X), TS(T))
formulas.text: r_T(X) rolls T back iff TS(T) < W-TS(X); else R-TS(X) ← max(R-TS(X), TS(T))

formulas.name: Timestamp ordering: write rule
formulas.tex: w_T(X) \text{ rolls back } T \iff TS(T) < R\text{-}TS(X) \lor TS(T) < W\text{-}TS(X); \text{ else } W\text{-}TS(X) \leftarrow TS(T)
formulas.text: w_T(X) rolls T back iff TS(T) < R-TS(X) or TS(T) < W-TS(X); else W-TS(X) ← TS(T)
formulas.note: Equality never causes a rollback: a transaction may read or rewrite its own write.

formulas.name: Thomas write rule
formulas.text: R-TS(X) ≤ TS(T) < W-TS(X) ⟹ ignore w_T(X) and continue
formulas.note: TS(T) < R-TS(X) still rolls T back; only the obsolete-write case changes.

formulas.name: Multiversion read rule
formulas.tex: r_T(X) \text{ returns } X_k, \quad W\text{-}TS(X_k) = \max\{\, W\text{-}TS(X_j) \le TS(T) \,\}
formulas.text: r_T(X) returns the version X_k with the largest W-TS(X_k) ≤ TS(T)
formulas.note: Reads never wait and never roll back under multiversion timestamp ordering.

formulas.name: Wait-die decision
formulas.tex: T_i \text{ requests from } T_j: \; TS(T_i) < TS(T_j) \Rightarrow T_i \text{ waits; else } T_i \text{ dies}
formulas.text: Ti requests a lock held by Tj: TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) ⇒ Ti waits; else Ti is rolled back

formulas.name: Wound-wait decision
formulas.tex: T_i \text{ requests from } T_j: \; TS(T_i) < TS(T_j) \Rightarrow T_j \text{ is wounded; else } T_i \text{ waits}
formulas.text: Ti requests a lock held by Tj: TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) ⇒ Tj is rolled back; else Ti waits
formulas.note: In both schemes the older transaction is never rolled back; only the younger one ever is.

formulas.name: 2PL serial order
formulas.tex: \text{lockpoint}(T_i) < \text{lockpoint}(T_j) \implies T_i \text{ precedes } T_j \text{ in the equivalent serial order}
formulas.text: lockpoint(Ti) < lockpoint(Tj) ⟹ Ti precedes Tj in the equivalent serial schedule

formulas.name: Write-ahead logging rule
formulas.tex: t(\text{log record of } X \text{ on disk}) < t(\text{page of } X \text{ on disk})
formulas.text: log record of an update is on stable storage before the data page it changes
formulas.note: Also: the commit record must be on disk before the transaction is reported committed.

complexity.name: Conflict-serializability test (precedence graph)
complexity.notes: m operations, n transactions, e edges: pairwise scan for conflicts, then DFS cycle detection in O(n + e).

complexity.name: View-serializability test
complexity.notes: The brute-force check compares the schedule against all n! serial orders.

problemTypes.title: Decide conflict serializability from a schedule
recipe: Write each item's operations in schedule order and mark every pair from different transactions with at least one write.
Add an edge from the earlier operation's transaction to the later one's for each such pair.
Look for a cycle; if none, read off the equivalent serial schedules as the topological orders.
problemTypes.trap: Checking only adjacent operations misses edges; two reads never add an edge.

problemTypes.title: View serializable but not conflict serializable
recipe: Run the precedence-graph test first; if acyclic, the schedule is also view serializable.
If cyclic and there is no blind write, stop: it is not view serializable.
Otherwise list initial reads, reads-from pairs and the final writer of each item, then test candidate serial orders against all three.
problemTypes.trap: A cyclic precedence graph does not settle view serializability when blind writes are present.

problemTypes.title: Classify a schedule as recoverable, cascadeless or strict
recipe: Find every dirty read: Tj reads X after Ti wrote it and before Ti committed. If Tj commits before Ti, the schedule is not recoverable.
If any dirty read exists, the schedule is not cascadeless.
If there is no dirty read, also look for dirty writes; none means strict.
problemTypes.trap: Recoverable only constrains commit order; a dirty read with the right commit order is still recoverable.

problemTypes.title: Which protocol guarantees which property
recipe: Serializability: every 2PL variant, timestamp ordering (conflict), Thomas rule (view only).
Deadlock freedom: conservative 2PL, timestamp ordering, wait-die, wound-wait; not basic, strict or rigorous 2PL.
Cascadelessness: strict and rigorous 2PL; not basic 2PL or basic timestamp ordering.
problemTypes.trap: Strict 2PL holds only X locks to commit, yet it can still deadlock.

problemTypes.title: Timestamp-ordering trace
recipe: Keep a small table of R-TS and W-TS per item, all starting at 0.
For each operation apply the read or write test, update the table, and stop at the first rollback.
Under the Thomas rule, a write with R-TS ≤ TS < W-TS is skipped, and the trace continues.
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting that a read raises R-TS only to the maximum, so an older reader leaves it unchanged.

problemTypes.title: Wait-die and wound-wait outcomes
recipe: Identify requester and holder and compare timestamps: smaller is older.
Wait-die: older requester waits, younger requester is rolled back.
Wound-wait: older requester rolls back the holder, younger requester waits.
problemTypes.trap: In wound-wait the victim is the holder, not the requester.

problemTypes.title: Recover the database from a log with a checkpoint
recipe: Split transactions into committed (commit record present) and uncommitted.
Undo uncommitted updates scanning backward, restoring each old value, all the way back to each loser's start.
Redo committed updates after the last checkpoint scanning forward; those committed before it are already on disk.
problemTypes.trap: Undoing the uncommitted updates in forward order leaves an intermediate value when two losers wrote the same item.

problemTypes.title: Count schedules or conflict-serializable schedules
recipe: Total interleavings: multinomial coefficient over the transactions' operation counts.
For conflict-serializable ones, find the conflicting pairs and keep only interleavings where every conflict points one way.
Count each direction separately and add, remembering the serial schedules are included.

questions.stem: Transaction T1 has 3 operations and transaction T2 has 3 operations. How many non-serial schedules of T1 and T2 are possible?
questions.explanation: Each transaction keeps its own order, so a schedule is a choice of which 3 of the 6 positions belong to T1: C(6, 3) = 20. Exactly 2 of them are serial (T1 T2 and T2 T1), leaving 20 − 2 = 18.

questions.stem: Consider the schedule S: r1(X); r2(Y); r1(Y); r2(X); w2(Y); w1(X); c1; c2. Which statement is correct?
options: S is conflict serializable, equivalent to T1 then T2
S is conflict serializable, equivalent to T2 then T1
S is view serializable but not conflict serializable
S is neither conflict serializable nor view serializable
questions.explanation: Conflicts: r1(Y) before w2(Y) gives T1 → T2; r2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 → T1. The precedence graph has a cycle, so S is not conflict serializable. Both writes follow a read of the same item by the same transaction, so there is no blind write; then view serializability coincides with conflict serializability. Directly: in T1 T2, T2 would read X written by T1, and in T2 T1, T1 would read Y written by T2, but in S both read initial values.

questions.stem: How many serial schedules are conflict equivalent to S: r1(X); w1(X); r2(X); r3(X); w3(Y); r4(Y); w4(Z)?
questions.explanation: Edges: w1(X)→r2(X) gives T1 → T2, w1(X)→r3(X) gives T1 → T3, and w3(Y)→r4(Y) gives T3 → T4. r2(X) and r3(X) are both reads, so no edge between T2 and T3. Topological orders: T1 first, then T2 placed anywhere relative to the chain T3 → T4: T1 T2 T3 T4, T1 T3 T2 T4, T1 T3 T4 T2. That is 3.

questions.stem: Consider S: r1(X); w2(X); w1(X); w3(X). Which of the following statements are true?
options: S is view equivalent to the serial schedule T1, T2, T3
S is view equivalent to the serial schedule T2, T1, T3
questions.explanation: r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 → T2 and w2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 → T1, a cycle, so S is not conflict serializable. In S, T1 reads the initial X and T3 writes X last. Serial T1, T2, T3 matches both (T2's blind write is overwritten unread), so S is view serializable. In T2, T1, T3, T1 would read T2's value of X instead of the initial one, so that order fails.

questions.stem: Classify the schedule S: r1(X); w1(X); r2(X); w2(X); c1; c2.
questions.explanation: T2 reads X after T1 wrote it and before c1: a dirty read, so S is not cascadeless (if T1 aborted, T2 would have to abort too). T1 commits before T2 commits, so the abort could still be handled: S is recoverable.

questions.stem: Which of the following hold for every schedule produced by strict two-phase locking?
options: No deadlock can occur while producing it
A transaction may release a shared lock before it commits
questions.explanation: Strict 2PL is 2PL, so its schedules are conflict serializable. Holding X locks until commit means nobody can read or overwrite uncommitted data, so schedules are cascadeless (in fact strict). It only restricts X locks, so S locks may go early in the shrinking phase. Its growing phase is ordinary 2PL, so two transactions requesting each other's locks still deadlock.

questions.stem: Which lock sequence for a single transaction obeys two-phase locking?
options: lock-S(A); read(A); unlock(A); lock-X(B); write(B); unlock(B)
lock-X(A); lock-S(B); read(B); write(A); unlock(A); unlock(B)
lock-S(A); read(A); lock-X(B); unlock(A); lock-X(C); write(B); write(C); unlock(B); unlock(C)
lock-X(A); write(A); unlock(A); lock-X(A); write(A); unlock(A)
questions.explanation: 2PL forbids any lock request after the first unlock. Sequence 2 acquires both locks before releasing anything. Sequence 1 locks B after unlocking A, sequence 3 locks C after unlocking A, and sequence 4 relocks A after unlocking it.

questions.stem: Under basic timestamp ordering, TS(T1) = 5, TS(T2) = 10, TS(T3) = 15, and every read and write timestamp starts at 0. The schedule is r1(A); r2(B); w2(A); w3(B); r2(A); w1(B). Which operation is the first to cause a rollback?
questions.explanation: r1(A): 5 ≥ W-TS(A) = 0, R-TS(A) = 5. r2(B): R-TS(B) = 10. w2(A): 10 ≥ R-TS(A) = 5 and ≥ W-TS(A) = 0, so W-TS(A) = 10. w3(B): 15 ≥ 10 and ≥ 0, W-TS(B) = 15. r2(A): 10 ≥ W-TS(A) = 10, fine (T2 reads its own write). w1(B): 5 < R-TS(B) = 10, so T1 is rolled back. The Thomas rule would not help, because the failure is against R-TS, not W-TS.

questions.stem: TS(T1) = 5 and TS(T2) = 10, with R-TS(X) = W-TS(X) = 0 initially. The schedule is r1(X); w2(X); w1(X). Under timestamp ordering with the Thomas write rule, what happens at w1(X)?
options: T1 is rolled back because TS(T1) < W-TS(X)
The write is ignored and T1 continues; X keeps the value T2 wrote
T2 is rolled back so that T1's write can be applied
The write is applied and W-TS(X) becomes 5
questions.explanation: After r1(X), R-TS(X) = 5; after w2(X), W-TS(X) = 10. At w1(X), TS(T1) = 5 is not less than R-TS(X) = 5, but it is less than W-TS(X) = 10. Basic TO would roll T1 back; the Thomas rule treats the write as obsolete, skips it, and lets T1 go on.

questions.stem: TS(T1) = 5, TS(T2) = 10, TS(T3) = 15. T2 holds an exclusive lock on Q. First T3 and then T1 request a lock on Q. Under wound-wait, what happens?
options: T3 is rolled back; T1 waits
T3 waits; T2 is rolled back and T1 gets the lock
T3 waits; T1 is rolled back
T3 is rolled back; T2 is rolled back and T1 gets the lock
questions.explanation: T3 is younger than the holder T2 (15 > 10), so it waits. T1 is older than T2 (5 < 10), so it wounds T2, which is rolled back and releases Q; T1 is granted the lock and T3 keeps waiting, now for T1. Under wait-die the outcome would be the reverse pattern: T3 dies and T1 waits.

questions.stem: Which of the following concurrency-control schemes can never deadlock?
questions.explanation: Conservative 2PL takes every lock before starting and waits holding none, so no hold-and-wait. Timestamp ordering never waits; it only proceeds or rolls back. Wait-die lets only older transactions wait for younger ones, so a cycle cannot form. Strict 2PL acquires locks incrementally and can deadlock exactly as basic 2PL does.

questions.stem: A system uses immediate update with undo/redo logging. The log at the crash is: <T1 start>; <T1, A, 100, 150>; <T2 start>; <T2, B, 200, 180>; <T1 commit>; <checkpoint {T2}>; <T3 start>; <T3, A, 150, 120>; <T2, C, 50, 70>; <T3 commit>; <T4 start>; <T4, B, 180, 300>. Records are <T, item, old, new>. After recovery, what is A + B + C?
questions.explanation: Committed: T1 (before the checkpoint, already on disk) and T3. Uncommitted: T2 and T4. Undo backward: T4's B ← 180, T2's C ← 50, T2's B ← 200. Redo after the checkpoint: T3's A ← 120. Final A = 120, B = 200, C = 50, so A + B + C = 370.

questions.stem: T1: r1(A); w1(A); r1(B); w1(B) and T2: r2(B); w2(B). How many of the possible schedules of T1 and T2 are conflict serializable?
questions.explanation: There are 6!/(4!·2!) = 15 schedules. Only B is shared. If both T2 operations come before r1(B), all conflicts give T2 → T1: the 2 operations go into the 3 gaps before r1(B) in C(4, 2) = 6 ways. If both come after w1(B), all give T1 → T2: 1 way. Any split of T2's operations around r1(B) or w1(B) creates edges in both directions. Total 6 + 1 = 7.

questions.stem: A transfer transaction executes write(A) with A reduced by 100 and the system crashes before write(B). On restart the debit to A is still visible. Which property has been violated?
questions.explanation: The transaction never committed, so all of its effects must disappear; leaving half of it in place breaks all-or-nothing execution. Durability concerns committed work, and isolation concerns interference between concurrent transactions.

questions.stem: Under the SQL standard's REPEATABLE READ isolation level, which anomaly can still occur?
options: Lost update of a row the transaction has read
questions.explanation: REPEATABLE READ keeps every row already read stable, which rules out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and lost updates on those rows. Rows newly inserted by others that match a predicate can still appear on a re-run query: phantoms. Only SERIALIZABLE excludes them.

questions.stem: Transaction T1 holds an IX lock on table R. Which lock on R can another transaction T2 be granted immediately?
questions.explanation: IX is compatible only with IS and IX. S would conflict with the X locks T1 intends to take on rows, SIX contains S, and X conflicts with everything.

pitfalls.text: Two reads of the same item never conflict, and operations of the same transaction never conflict; neither adds a precedence edge.
Build the precedence graph from all conflicting pairs, not only adjacent operations.
2PL guarantees conflict serializability, not deadlock freedom; only conservative 2PL is deadlock-free.
Strict 2PL holds X locks until commit; rigorous 2PL holds all locks until commit. Read the question for which one is meant.
Wait-die and wound-wait are easy to swap: the younger transaction is the one rolled back in both, but in wound-wait the victim is the lock holder.
Recoverable does not imply cascadeless: a dirty read with the writer committing first is recoverable yet still cascades on abort.
WAL means the log record goes to disk before the data page, never the reverse.
Under timestamp ordering a restarted transaction needs a new timestamp; keeping the old one is the wait-die and wound-wait rule.

revisionCard.heading: Serializability
lines: Conflict: different T, same item, at least one write
Conflict serializable ⟺ precedence graph acyclic; serial order = topological order
View: same initial reads, reads-from, final writes
View but not conflict ⇒ blind write present; view test is NP-complete
Schedules of n1, …, nk ops: (Σnᵢ)!/Πnᵢ!; serial ones: k!

revisionCard.heading: Recoverability
lines: Recoverable: the writer commits before the reader commits
Strict: no read or write of X until its writer ends

revisionCard.heading: Protocols
lines: 2PL: growing then shrinking; serial order = lock points; can deadlock
Strict 2PL: X till commit; rigorous: all till commit; conservative: all upfront, no deadlock
TO read: TS < W-TS ⇒ roll back; write: TS < R-TS or TS < W-TS ⇒ roll back
Thomas: R-TS ≤ TS < W-TS ⇒ ignore write
Wait-die: old waits, young dies. Wound-wait: old wounds holder, young waits

lines: WAL: log before data, commit record before commit
Redo committed after the checkpoint, undo uncommitted backward
ARIES: analysis, redo (repeat history), undo with CLRs

errata.claim: w1(X); w2(X); w3(X) is offered as a schedule that is view serializable but not conflict serializable.
errata.correction: Its precedence graph has only T1 → T2, T2 → T3 and T1 → T3, which is acyclic, so it is conflict serializable (equivalent to T1, T2, T3). A correct example needs a read that creates a cycle, such as r1(X); w2(X); w1(X); w3(X), which is view equivalent to T1, T2, T3 but not conflict serializable.

errata.claim: The 2PL comparison table marks strict 2PL as not producing strict schedules.
errata.correction: Strict 2PL holds every exclusive lock until commit or abort, so no other transaction can read or write an item written by an uncommitted transaction: its schedules are strict, as stated on page 593. Rigorous 2PL differs by also holding shared locks, which makes the serialization order equal the commit order.

errata.claim: Starvation under timestamp ordering is mitigated by re-using the transaction's timestamp on restart.
errata.correction: A transaction rolled back by timestamp ordering must restart with a new, larger timestamp; with its old timestamp it would fail the same test again, because the item timestamps that rejected it only grow. Keeping the original timestamp is the starvation fix for wait-die and wound-wait.
